title: A Sam Altman parody offers an amusing lesson in memory management
gist: Developer Iain Kay's parody Bash script 'Ram-Altman' emails Sam Altman once a day when over 10% of a PC's RAM is available, mocking Altman's Cheeky Pint remark that consumer DRAM sitting idle in personal computers is a poor global allocation. The piece doubles as a lesson in how Linux reports available versus free memory.

insights.claim: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman argued on the Cheeky Pint podcast with Stripe's John Collison that local inference on personal computers is globally inefficient because scarce DRAM sits in consumer PCs used only about 5 percent of the time instead of in data centers.
insights.speaker: Nick Indge
insights.so_what: Signals the frontier-lab view that DRAM supply should flow to data centers, consistent with tight memory markets and cloud-over-local inference strategy.
insights.quote: from a global allocation perspective, actually, it’s quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world’s limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer
insights.locator: As reported by The Verge, on the October 29 episode

insights.claim: Altman's comment that DRAM in personal PCs is wasteful drew a viral backlash; he said the remarks were taken out of context, posted 'i want you to have so much ram', and briefly renamed himself 'RAM Altman' on X.
insights.speaker: Nick Indge
insights.so_what: Consumer sensitivity to AI data centers crowding out PC memory supply is a live reputational issue for AI labs.
insights.locator: Altman has since explained that his comments were taken out of context

insights.claim: Iain Kay's open-source Ram-Altman Bash script polls /proc/meminfo every five minutes and sends at most one joke email per day when more than 10 percent of system RAM is available, with a dry-run mode and no recipient addresses included to avoid harassment.
insights.speaker: Nick Indge
insights.so_what: Mostly a cultural signal: developer sentiment toward OpenAI's stance on local compute is skeptical and mocking.
insights.quote: --dry-run is the best way to enjoy this. It costs nothing and all the jokes are there.
insights.locator: Users can schedule the script to ask the kernel

insights.claim: The Ram-Altman project concedes that Altman was talking about how much of the time memory is utilized, while the script only measures instantaneous free capacity, so it does not actually rebut his utilization argument.
insights.speaker: Nick Indge
insights.so_what: The underlying utilization critique of idle consumer hardware stands even if the framing was unpopular.
insights.locator: The project concedes the nuance that Altman was referring

insights.claim: Linux's reported 'free' RAM understates usable memory because the kernel fills spare RAM with reclaimable file caches; MemAvailable is the kernel's estimate of memory it can hand over without swapping, so used memory is best computed as MemTotal minus MemAvailable.
insights.speaker: Nick Indge
insights.so_what: Useful for capacity planning: naive 'free' metrics overstate memory pressure on Linux hosts.
insights.locator: If the script only showed what Linux reports as “free” RAM

insights.claim: On a 16 GiB Fedora 44 KDE desktop, the kernel exposes 14.9 GiB usable, and Ram-Altman measured 10 GiB used with 4.9 GiB (33.1 percent) available versus only 1.8 GiB shown as 'free'.
insights.speaker: Nick Indge
insights.so_what: Illustrates typical desktop headroom — roughly a third of RAM available at a given moment.
insights.locator: A test run of the script on my Fedora 44 KDE machine
